title: What the heck is a hiccup?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore hiccups: Chuck attempts to induce hiccups by chugging a Barq's root beer, then listener Jess's question about personal hiccup patterns. They cover intractable and persistent hiccups, theories on why humans hiccup (Galen's angry-emotions idea, a 2003 amphibian gill-ventilation/relic theory, the fetal recapitulation theory, premature babies hiccupping more), the physiology involving the phrenic nerve, diaphragm and epiglottis, common triggers (overeating, spicy food, smoking, alcohol, temperature changes, stress), medical treatments (chlorpromazine, medical marijuana, surgery, stomach emptying), folk cures and why they may work (interrupting the respiratory cycle, stimulating the nasopharynx, distraction), record-long hiccup cases such as Charles Osborne, Jennifer Mee and others, and a listener email from an Australian fan.

segments.title: Opening banter and root beer hiccup attempt
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode on hiccups. Chuck attempts to give himself hiccups by chugging a root beer, without success.

segments.title: Listener question on hiccup patterns
segments.summary: Listener Jess asks about hiccups. The hosts mention that people may have a personal hiccup pattern, that hiccup spells usually last minutes to hours, and that Chuck and Josh have their own cures.

segments.title: Intractable and persistent hiccups
segments.summary: Hiccups lasting over 48 hours are called persistent, and those lasting over a month are intractable; intractable hiccups are prevalent among AIDS patients. A Spanish patient reportedly had his hiccups cured by marijuana, which returned 24 hours later.

segments.title: Theories on why we hiccup
segments.summary: No one knows why humans hiccup. Galen proposed angry emotions from the stomach; researchers at Salpêtrière Hospital in 2003 proposed hiccups are a relic of amphibian gill ventilation; the recapitulation theory suggests fetuses use hiccups before lungs develop. Premature babies hiccup more, and hormones may play a role.

segments.title: Physiology of a hiccup
segments.summary: The phrenic nerve controls the diaphragm; irritation causes diaphragm spasms producing a quick breath, and the epiglottis closing produces the hiccup sound. The vagus nerve can also be involved. The breathing path is described.

segments.title: Triggers of hiccups
segments.summary: Causes include overeating, spicy or hot food, smoking and excessive drinking, rapid temperature changes in the stomach, and stress, emotion, and possibly mental illness. Chlorpromazine, an antipsychotic, can cure long-term hiccups.

segments.title: Josh's hiccup story and Flaming Lips
segments.summary: Josh recounts having hiccups for about six hours after drinking at a Flaming Lips show in Athens. Wayne Coyne's reaction is joked about.

segments.title: Home remedies and medical treatments
segments.summary: Mental distraction and home remedies such as drinking from the far side of a glass, biting a lemon, tongue-pulling, and tickling the roof of the mouth work by stimulating the nasopharynx. Breathing tricks like the paper bag or holding breath interrupt the respiratory cycle. Medical options include seeing a doctor after 48 hours, neck massage, carotid pressure, surgery to disconnect the phrenic nerve, and stomach emptying by tube. Warnings are given against pressing the eyeball.

segments.title: Record and long-lasting hiccup cases
segments.summary: Charles Osborne reportedly hiccupped from 1922 to 1990 (about 430 million hiccups, per Guinness). Jennifer Mee hiccupped for five weeks in 2007. Jamie hiccupped for eight months, and David Willis had two unsuccessful surgeries for a five-year bout.

segments.title: Listener email from a fan in Australia
segments.summary: A listener from Wagga Wagga, Australia, now in Sydney, writes a playful email about the hosts' selection preferences and his desire to be read on air.
